analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors, and it died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Social Security 2100 Act would raise every beneficiary's check, switch cost-of-living adjustments to a price index built for seniors' spending, and set a higher minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages. It would also lift the income cap that stops Social Security taxes at a certain salary level, so wages above $400,000 would be taxed, and payroll tax rates would rise slowly over decades. The bill raised benefits and the money to pay for them, but it never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries get a roughly 3% benefit bump, a COLA that tracks what seniors actually buy, and a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line for long-career low earners [S2, S3]. Middle-income retirees keep more of their benefits because the income threshold for taxing them doubles ($25,000 to $50,000 single; $32,000 to $100,000 joint) [S2, S3]. People with disabilities benefit from a reallocation of payroll revenue to the Disability Insurance trust fund [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the benefit formula factor from 90% to 93%, an across-the-board increase for all beneficiaries beginning with benefits payable after December 2015 [S2, S3].
Switches annual cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the spending of older households [S2, S3].
Creates a new special minimum benefit tied to the poverty line, rising with years worked up to 125% of the poverty amount for workers with 30+ years, aimed at lifetime low earners [S3].
Doubles the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable, from $25,000 to $50,000 for singles and $32,000 to $100,000 for joint filers [S2, S3].

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to all wage and self-employment income above $400,000, which today escapes the tax, and gradually raises the tax rate from 6.2% to 7.65% each for employees and employers through 2084 [S2, S3].
Reallocates a larger share of payroll tax revenue to the Disability Insurance trust fund, whose financing was projected to run short in 2016 [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wages above $400,000 would be newly subject to the Social Security tax, falling on the roughly 1% of earners above that level and on their employers, who pay a matching share [S2, S3]. Every worker and employer would also see the combined tax rate rise one-twentieth of a point per year starting in 2018, eventually reaching 15.3% total by 2084 [S2, S3]. Higher-income retirees whose benefits remain taxable would continue to pay tax on up to 85% of them [S3].

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase applies to nearly all workers and employers, not just the wealthy: the rate rises steadily from 2018 to 2084, and employers' matching share may be passed back to workers as slower wage growth [S2, S3].
Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer shares, so their combined rate climbs from 12.4% toward 15.3% [S3].

Raising benefits and taxes at the same time means the plan's full cost lands on the next several decades of workers; a good-faith objection is that payroll taxes are regressive at the bottom even after the new minimum benefit partially offsets that [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and concrete: a universal increase, a senior-specific inflation index, and a poverty-line floor for the lowest earners, with the largest new tax burden aimed at income above $400,000 that currently escapes Social Security tax. The trade-off is a slow, permanent tax increase touching every covered worker and their employers over about 70 years. Critics who oppose any payroll tax increase would argue the plan grows the program's tax base rather than trimming benefits; the bill's design, by pricing the expansion with its own revenue, addresses the common objection that expansions are unpaid for. The main weakness is political, not design: it drew no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill on July 30, 2015 [S1, S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, its only action in the Congress [S5].
It ended the Congress with zero cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any committee action or vote, high earners above $400,000 and their employers avoided the new payroll tax on that income, and the current benefit formula, tax rates, and taxing thresholds for beneficiaries stayed unchanged [S2, S5].

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act and had it read twice and referred to the Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 30, 2015 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the 114th Congress

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4]; with no votes held, no roll-call split exists, and the only recorded action was referral to a Republican-chaired committee that never acted [S5].

industries.note: The bill would remove the cap that currently exempts all wages above the annual ceiling from Social Security tax, taxing income above $400,000 instead. Their added tax is what funds the benefit increases ordinary beneficiaries receive.

Employers pay a matching share of Social Security tax, so both the new tax on wages above $400,000 and the gradual rate increase to 7.65% raise labor costs. Higher earners with large payrolls would absorb the largest increases.
Self-employment income above $400,000 would be newly taxed, and the combined self-employment rate would climb from 12.4% to 15.3% by 2084, hitting high-earning professionals hardest.

All current and future beneficiaries would receive larger checks, a senior-specific inflation adjustment, and protection of more of their benefits from income tax; low lifetime earners gain the most through the poverty-line minimum benefit.
